questions.q: Why does Mara run `secedit /export` before and after changing the account lockout policy?
options: It's required for `net accounts` to work at all
To create a before/after record proving exactly what changed, which goes into the documentation
It encrypts the local security policy
It disables the RemoteRegistry service automatically
questions.explain: "I configured it" isn't the same as "I confirmed it" — the before/after export is the concrete proof that the lockout policy change actually landed.

questions.q: Why is RemoteRegistry a good example of what to disable on HRU-FILE01 and HRU-APP01?
options: Because it's required for LAPS to function
Because it has legitimate uses elsewhere but neither server needs it, so leaving it enabled is unused attack surface
Because it's the service that enforces the Domain firewall profile
Because disabling it is required before SMB can work
questions.explain: A baseline closes gaps like this: a service with no real purpose on a given machine is one more thing an attacker could try to use if they ever reach the box.

questions.q: What problem does moving both servers to LAPS actually solve?
options: It speeds up the file-sharing service
Both servers were sharing one local admin password, so a compromise of one was effectively a compromise of both; LAPS gives each machine its own rotated password
It replaces the need for an account lockout policy
It opens the Domain firewall profile automatically
questions.explain: A shared local admin password means one leaked credential grants access to every machine sharing it. LAPS generates and rotates a unique password per server.

questions.q: Why does Mara leave the Private and Public Windows Firewall profiles at default deny instead of writing rules for them?
options: Because Windows doesn't allow custom rules on those profiles
Because HRU-FILE01 and HRU-APP01 only ever connect to the network as domain members, so those profiles will never legitimately apply, and an unused profile locked to deny is itself a control
Because the Domain profile covers all three profiles automatically
Because LAPS manages those profiles instead
questions.explain: A server that will never be on a Private or Public network doesn't need rules for them — leaving them at default deny is a deliberate decision, not an oversight.

questions.q: What does `gpresult /r` confirm that simply configuring a setting does not?
options: That the server has internet access
Which policies actually took effect on the machine, verifying the configuration really applied rather than just being saved somewhere
The current LAPS password
The number of failed sign-in attempts today
questions.explain: Verification is the whole point of this lesson's method — gpresult /r shows what actually applied, closing the gap between "configured" and "confirmed."
